stem: A 45-year-old woman who sings professionally has weakness of one cricothyroid muscle after a thyroidectomy and can no longer raise her pitch. Her vocal cords move normally and she is not hoarse.
oneliner: 45F + singer + after thyroid surgery cannot raise pitch + cricothyroid weakness + cords move normally → which pharyngeal arch?
ask: The injured nerve belongs to which pharyngeal arch?

whyNot.A: The 1st arch nerve is the **mandibular division of the trigeminal**, supplying the muscles of mastication, not the larynx
whyNot.B: The 2nd arch nerve is the **facial nerve**, supplying the muscles of facial expression
whyNot.C: The 3rd arch nerve is the **glossopharyngeal**, supplying only the stylopharyngeus
whyNot.E: The 6th arch nerve is the **recurrent laryngeal**, which moves the other laryngeal muscles; her **cords move normally** and she is **not hoarse**

answer: 4th pharyngeal arch (superior laryngeal nerve, from the vagus)
why: The cricothyroid is supplied by the **superior laryngeal nerve**, the nerve of the **4th pharyngeal arch**. The other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the **recurrent laryngeal nerve of the 6th arch**, which is why her cords move normally and she is not hoarse.

idea.rule: 4th arch = superior laryngeal nerve (cricothyroid, pharyngeal constrictors, levator veli palatini); 6th arch = recurrent laryngeal nerve (other intrinsic laryngeal muscles).
also: Both laryngeal nerves are branches of the vagus nerve
The right recurrent nerve hooks under the right subclavian (4th arch artery); the left hooks under the ligamentum arteriosum (6th arch)
The 6th arch artery forms the pulmonary arteries and the ductus arteriosus
The 4th arch artery forms the aortic arch on the left and the proximal right subclavian on the right
